title: Perceived value versus actual usefulness
definition: What the product appears to offer must match what it measurably does for the user's job. Value is demonstrated by a result the user can see and check, not asserted by copy, visuals or pricing cues.
intended_outcome: A user can point to a concrete thing the product did for them, and every stated benefit is backed by a feature present in the build.
implementation_guidance: Bind each headline benefit to a product behaviour and a checkable result in the same flow. A benefit with no corresponding feature in the build is a finding.
Show what changed for automated actions, and keep a log of what the system did on the user's behalf.
Title each dashboard figure with the question it answers and state its source. Retire figures nobody uses (see brain.design.md section 2).
An upgrade prompt names the specific capability gained and never interrupts a task in progress.
Value never overrides correctness: a polished wrong number is worse than no number.

automated: Claim-to-feature trace: each claim in copy matches a present route or feature (heuristic, flagged for human review).
expert_review: Walk the primary job end to end and note where value is asserted but not shown.
observed_behaviour: Task completion with a correct result on the primary job (usability test or telemetry; n recorded).
customer_feedback: Ask what the product did for the user the last time they used it, in their words.

limitations: Perceived value is subjective and context-dependent.
Automated claim tracing is heuristic and will miss implied claims.

evidence.summary: Dot Intelligence Manifesto principle 3: every recommendation is measurable; define the metric before the feature.
Binding every benefit claim to a shown result lowers the gap between what is promised and what is delivered.
evidence.rationale: Reasoned from the claim-versus-feature mismatches this engine is built to find; no Dot measurement of the effect exists.
